In such idolatry the idol or animal was, with regard to the majority, the ultimate object of worship. Some professed to regard the visible image as a mere symbol of the real object of their adoration; while others believed that the gods in some way filled these idols, and operated through them; and others again, that the universal principle of being was reverenced under these manifestations. The Scriptures take no account of these destinations. All who bowed down to stocks and stones are denounced as worshipping gods which their own hands had made; and idolatry is made to include not merely the worship of false gods, but the worship of the true God by images. The universal prevalence of idolatry among the heathens, notwithstanding the revelation which God had made of himself in his works, is the evidence which Paul adduces to prove that they are ungodly, and consequently exposed to that wrath which is revealed against all ungodliness. In the following, verses, to the end of the chapter, he shows that they are unrighteous; that as the consequence of their departure from God, they sank into the grossest vices.

<!-- PAGE 62 -->
VERSE 24. <span style="color:#800000">*Wherefore also he gave them*</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*in their lusts*</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*unto uncleanness.*</span> The most natural construction of this passage is to connect <span style="color:#0000d4">εἰς</span> <span style="color:#0000d4">ἀκαθαρσίαν</span> with <span style="color:#0000d4">παρέδωκεν</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*he gave up unto uncleanness.*</span> We have the same construction in vers. 26, 28, and infrequently elsewhere. To construct <span style="color:#0000d4">παρέδωκεν</span> with <span style="color:#0000d4">ἐν</span> <span style="color:#0000d4">ταῖς</span> <span style="color:#0000d4">ἐπιθυμίαις</span>, as Beza and others do, gives indeed a good sense, <span style="color:#800000">*He gave them up to their desires unto uncleanness*</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*i.e*</span>., so that they became unclean, but is opposed to the constant usage of the New Testament, in as much as <span style="color:#0000d4">παραδίδωμι</span> never occurs in construction with <span style="color:#0000d4">ἐν</span>. If the former construction be adopted, <span style="color:#0000d4">ἐν</span> <span style="color:#0000d4">ταῖς</span> <span style="color:#0000d4">ἐπιθυμίαις</span> may be rendered as in our version, <span style="color:#800000">*through*</span> their lusts; or better in their lusts; <span style="color:#0000d4">ἐν</span> expressing their condition, or circumstances; <span style="color:#800000">*them in their lusts*</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*i.e.*</span>, being in them, immersed in them. <span style="color:#800000">*To dishonor*</span>, <span style="color:#0000d4">τοῦ</span> <span style="color:#0000d4">ἀτιμάζεσθαι</span>. This infinitive with <span style="color:#0000d4">τοῦ</span> may depend on the preceding noun; ‘the uncleanness of dishonoring,’ etc., “quae cernebatur in,” etc. <span style="color:#800000">*Winer*</span>, § 45:4. <span style="color:#800000">*b*</span>. But as the infinitive with the genitive article is so frequently used to express design, or simple sequence, it is better to make it depend on the whole preceding clause, ‘He gave them up to uncleanness, to dishonor,’ i.e., either in order that they might dishonor, or <span style="color:#800000">*so that*</span> they dishonored, etc. <span style="color:#0000d4">ἀτιμὰζεσθαι</span> may be taken either as middle, <span style="color:#800000">*so that they dishonored their bodies*</span>; or as passive, <span style="color:#800000">*so that their bodies were dishonored.*</span> The former best suits the context. ’<span style="color:#0000d4">Εν</span> <span style="color:#0000d4">ἐαυτοῖς</span> is either equivalent to <span style="color:#0000d4">ἐν</span> <span style="color:#0000d4">ἀλλήλοις</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*reciprocally*</span>, they dishonored one another, as to their bodies; or <span style="color:#800000">*in themselves*</span>, dishonoring their bodies in themselves; “significantius exprimit,” says Calvin, “quam profundas et ineluibiles ignominiae notas corporibus suis inusserint.”

<!-- PAGE 63 -->
This abandonment of the heathen to the dominion of sin is represented as a punitive infliction. They forsook God, <span style="color:#0000d4">διὸ</span> <span style="color:#0000d4">καί</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*wherefore also*</span> he gave them up to uncleanness. This is explained as a simple permission on the part of God. But it removes no real difficulty. If God permits those who forsake him to sink into vice, he does it intelligently and intentionally. The language of the apostle, as well as the analogy of Scripture, demands more than this. It is at least a judicial abandonment. It is as a punishment for their apostasy that God gives men up to the power of sin. Tradidit Deus ut justus judex. He withdraws from the wicked the restraints of his providence and grace, and gives them over to the dominion of sin. God is presented in the Bible as the absolute moral and physical ruler of the world. He governs all things according, to the counsel of his own will and the nature of his creatures. What happens as consequences does not come by chance, but as designed; and the sequence is secured by his control. “It is beyond question,” says Tholuck, “that, according to the doctrine of the Old and New Testaments, sin is the punishment of sin.” So the Rabbins teach, “The reward of a good deed is a good deed, and of an evil deed, an evil deed.” This is also the teaching of all experience. We see that sin follows sin as an avenger. De Wette truly says, “Diese Ansicht ist nicht bloss jüdisch, sondern allgemein wahr vom absoluten Standpunkte der Religion aus.” “This is no mere Jewish doctrine, but it is universally true from the absolute standpoint of religion.” God is not a mere idle spectator of the order of events; he is at once the moral governor and efficient controller of all things. “Man is not ‘a virtue-machine,’” says Meyer, “when God rewards virtue with virtue; neither is he ‘a sin machine,’ when God punishes sin with sin.” Men are as free in sinning as they are in obeying; and what in one passage and from one point of view, is properly presented as the work of God, in another passage and from another point of view, is no less properly presented as the work of man. What is here said to be God’s work, in Ephesians 4:19 is declared to be the sinner’s own work.

<!-- PAGE 64 -->
VERSE 25. Who change (<span style="color:#0000d4">οἵτινες</span>). The pronoun has a causal sense, <span style="color:#800000">*being such as those who*</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*i.e.*</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*because they exchanged the*</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*truth of God for a lie*</span>. The construction is the same as in ver. 23, <span style="color:#0000d4">μετήλλαξαν ἐν</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*they exchanged for*</span>, not <span style="color:#800000">*they changed into*</span>. <span style="color:#800000">*The truth of God*</span>, either a periphrase for the true God, or the truth concerning God, i.e., right conceptions of God. <span style="color:#800000">*For a lie*</span>, that is, either a false God, or falsehood, i.e., false views of God. The former is the better explanation. The glory of God is God himself as glorious, and the truth of God, in this connection, is God himself as true; that is, the true God. In the Old Testament, as in Jeremiah 13:25; 16:19, the gods of the heathen are spoken of as lies. Anything which is not what it pretends to be, or what it is supposed to be, is in the Scriptures called a lie. The proof of this apostasy is, that <span style="color:#800000">*they worshipped*</span> (<span style="color:#0000d4">ἐσεβάσθησαν</span>) and served (<span style="color:#0000d4">ἐλάτρευσαν</span>). These words are often synonymous, both being used to express inward reverence and outward worship; although the former properly expresses the feeling, and the latter the outward service. The creature (<span style="color:#0000d4">κτίσει</span>), not the creation, but any particular created thing. This noun belongs, in sense, to both the preceding verbs, although the first by itself would require the accusative<span style="color:#800000">*. More than the Creator*</span>, <span style="color:#0000d4">παρὰ</span> <span style="color:#0000d4">τὸν</span> <span style="color:#0000d4">κτίσαντα</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*i.e.*</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*beyond*</span>, in the sense of more than, or in the sense of passing by, neglecting; “praeterito Creatore,” as Beza translates. The latter suits best. <span style="color:#800000">*Who is blessed for ever: Amen.*</span> Who, notwithstanding the neglect of the heathen, is the ever-blessed God. This is the natural tribute of reverence toward the God whom men dishonored by their idolatry. The word <span style="color:#0000d4">ἐυλογντός</span> is by Harless, Ephesians 1:3, and by Meyer, made to mean praised, as the Hebrew <span style="color:#008080">˚WrB;</span>, to which it so constantly answers; not, therefore, worthy of praise, but who is in fact the object of praise to all holy beings. Bretschneider (Lexicon), Tholuck, and others, render it “celebrandus, venerandus.” <span style="color:#800000">*Amen*</span> is properly a Hebrew adjective, signifying true or faithful. At the beginning of a sentence it is often used adverbially, verily, assuredly; at the end of a sentence it is used to express assent, <span style="color:#800000">*it is true*</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*so let it be*</span>. Paul says Amen to the declaration that God is the ever-blessed.

VERSE 26. <span style="color:#800000">*For this cause*</span>, etc. That is, because they worshipped the creature rather than the Creator, God gave them up to corrupt affections. <span style="color:#0000d4">Πάθη ἀτιμίας</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*shameful lusts*</span>, passions which are degrading, and the indulgence of which covers men with ignominy. This verse is therefore an amplification of the idea expressed in ver. 24. The reasons why Paul refers in the first instance to the sins of uncleanness, in illustration and proof of the degradation of the heathen, probably were, that those sins are always intimately connected with idolatry, forming at times even a, part of the service rendered to the false gods; that in turning from God and things spiritual, men naturally sink into the sensual; that the sins in question are peculiarly degrading; and that they were the most notorious, prevalent, and openly acknowledged of all the crimes of the heathen world. This corruption of morals was condemned to no one class or sex. The description given by profane writers of the moral corruption of the ante-Christian ages, is in all respects as revolting as that presented by the apostle. Of this the citations of Western and Grotius furnish abundant proof. Paul first refers to the degradation of females among the heathen, because they are always the last to be affected in the decay of morals, and their corruption is therefore proof that all virtue is lost.

VERSE 27. The apostle for the third time repeats the idea that the moral degradation of the heathen was a punishment of their apostasy from God. <span style="color:#800000">*Receiving*</span>, he says, <span style="color:#800000">*in themselves the meet recompense of their error*</span>. It is obvious from the whole context that <span style="color:#0000d4">πλάνη</span> here refers to the sin of forsaking the true God; and it is no less obvious that the recompense or punishment of this apostasy was the moral degradation which he had just described.

<!-- PAGE 65 -->
The heathen themselves did not fail to see the intimate connection between impiety and vice. <span style="color:#800000">*Silius*</span>, 4:794. “Heu primae scelerum causae mortalibus aegris naturam nescire Deum.” C<span style="color:#800000">*icero*</span> De natura Deorum, 12. “Haud scio, an, pietate adversus Deos sublatâ, fides etiam et societas, et una excellentissima virtus justitia tollatur.” See WETSTEIN. Those therefore who would merge religion into morality, or who suppose that morality can be sustained without religion, are more ignorant than the heathen. They not only shut their eyes to all the teachings both of philosophy and of history, but array against themselves the wrath of God, who has revealed his purpose to abandon to the most degrading lusts those who apostatize from him.

VERSE 28. <span style="color:#800000">*And as they did not think it worth while to retain God in their knowledge*</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*he gave them up to a reprobate mind*</span>. Another repetition of the sentiment is expressed in vers. 24, 26, that God abandons those who abandon him. <span style="color:#800000">*And as*</span>, <span style="color:#0000d4">καὶ</span> <span style="color:#0000d4">καθώς</span>. The cases are parallel; as they deserted God, so God abandoned them; comp. John 17:2. <span style="color:#800000">*They did not like*</span>, <span style="color:#0000d4">οὐκ</span> <span style="color:#0000d4">ἐδοκίμασαν</span>; the verb means to try or put to the test, to examine, to approve, and, <span style="color:#800000">*dignum habere*</span>, to regard as worthy, 1 Corinthians 16:3; 1 Thessalonians 2:4, and when followed by an infinitive, to <span style="color:#800000">*think it worth while*</span>. The heathen did not think it worth the trouble to retain the knowledge of God. They considered religion as useless, and supposed they could live without God. The phrase <span style="color:#0000d4">έχειν</span> <span style="color:#0000d4">ἐν</span> <span style="color:#0000d4">ἐπιγνώσει</span> is stronger than simply <span style="color:#800000">*to know*</span>; both because <span style="color:#0000d4">ἐπίγνωσις</span> <span style="color:#800000">*full knowledge*</span>, is stronger than <span style="color:#0000d4">γνῶσις</span>, and because <span style="color:#0000d4">έχειν</span> <span style="color:#0000d4">ἐν</span> <span style="color:#0000d4">ἐπιγνώσει</span> is stronger than <span style="color:#0000d4">ἐπιγιγνώσκειν</span>. The text therefore means <span style="color:#800000">*to retain in accurate or practical knowledge*</span>. It was the practical recognition of the only true God, whose eternal power and Godhead are revealed in his works, that men were unwilling constantly to make. <span style="color:#800000">*God gave them up to a reprobate mind*</span>. Beza, Bengel, and others, give <span style="color:#0000d4">ἀδόκιμος</span> here the sense of <span style="color:#800000">*judicii expers*</span>, incapable of judgment or discernment. But this is contrary to usage, and contrary to the etymology of the word. <span style="color:#0000d4">Δόκιμος</span> from <span style="color:#0000d4">δέχομαι</span>, means <span style="color:#800000">*receivable*</span>, worthy of being received; and <span style="color:#0000d4">ἀδόκιμος</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*worthy of rejection*</span>, reprobate<span style="color:#800000">*. To do things not becoming*</span>; that is, to do things not becoming the nature and duties of man. Of the things meant, the following verses contain a long, and painful catalogue. <span style="color:#0000d4">Ποιεῖν</span> is the exegetical infinitive, <span style="color:#800000">*to do*</span>, that is, <span style="color:#800000">*so that they did*</span>. It expresses the consequence of the dereliction just spoken of, and the natural fruit of a reprobate mind.

<!-- PAGE 66 -->
VERSES 29-31<span style="color:#800000">*. Being filled with all unrighteousness*</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*fornication*</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*wickedness*</span>, etc. The accusative <span style="color:#0000d4">πεπληρωμένους</span> is connected with <span style="color:#0000d4">αὐτοὺς</span> of the preceding verse. <span style="color:#800000">*He gave them up*</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*filled with all righteousness*</span>; or it depends on the preceding infinitive <span style="color:#0000d4">ποιεῖν</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*so that*</span> <span style="color:#800000">*they*</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*filled with all unrighteousness*</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*should commit*</span>, etc. It is not so connected with <span style="color:#0000d4">παρέδωκεν</span> as to imply that God gave them up after they were thus corrupt, but it is so connected with <span style="color:#0000d4">ποιεῖν</span> as to express the consequence of God’s abandoning them to do the things which are not convenient. The crimes here mentioned were not of rare occurrence. The heathen were filled with them. They not only abounded, but in many cases were palliated and even justified. Dark as the picture here drawn is, it is not so dark as that presented by the most distinguished Greek and Latin authors, of their own countrymen. Commentators have collected a fearful array of passages from the ancient writers, which more than sustain the account given by the apostle. We select a single passage from, Senca de Ira, 2:8: “Omnia sceleribus ac vitiis plena sunt; plus committitur quam quod possit coercitione sanari. Certatur ingenti quodam nequitiae, certamine; major quotidie peccandi cupiditas, minor verecundia est. Expulso melioris aequiorisque respectn, quocunque visum est, libido se impingit; nec furtiva jam scelera sunt, praeter oculos eunt. Adeoque in publicum missa nequitia est, et in omnium pectoribus evaluit, ut ionocentia non rara, sed nulla sit. Numquid enim singuli aut panci rupere legenm undique, velut signo dato, ad fas nefasque miscendum coorti sunt.” What Paul says of the ancient heathen world, is found to be true in all its essential features of men of all generations. Wherever men have existed, there have they shown themselves to be sinners, ungodly and unrighteous, and therefore justly exposed to the wrath of God. Of the vices with which the heathen were filled, <span style="color:#0000d4">πορνεία</span> stands first as the most prominent; <span style="color:#0000d4">πονρία</span> <span style="color:#800000">*malice*</span>, the disposition to inflict evil; <span style="color:#0000d4">πλεονεξία</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*rapacity*</span>, the desire to have more than is our due; <span style="color:#0000d4">κακία</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*malignity*</span>, malice in exercise; <span style="color:#0000d4">φθόνος</span> and <span style="color:#0000d4">φόνος</span> <span style="color:#800000">*envy*</span> and <span style="color:#800000">*murder*</span>, united either from similarity in sound or because the former tends to the latter; <span style="color:#0000d4">έρις</span> <span style="color:#0000d4">δόλος</span> <span style="color:#800000">*contention*</span> and <span style="color:#800000">*fraud*</span>, nearly related evils. The primary meaning of <span style="color:#0000d4">δόλος</span> is a bait, food exposed to entrap an animal; then the disposition to deceive, or an act of deception; <span style="color:#0000d4">κακοήθεια</span> (<span style="color:#0000d4">κακός</span> and <span style="color:#0000d4">η̈θος</span>) <span style="color:#800000">*malevolence*</span>, the disposition to make the worst of everything; <span style="color:#0000d4">ψιθυριστής</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*a whisperer*</span>, clandestine slanderer; <span style="color:#0000d4">κατάλαλος</span> <span style="color:#800000">*a detractor*</span>, one who speaks against others; <span style="color:#0000d4">θεστυγής</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*hateful to God*</span>, or <span style="color:#800000">*hating God*</span>. Usage is in favor of the passive sense, the connection of the active. All wicked men, and not any one particular class, are the objects of the divine displeasure. To meet this difficulty, Meyer proposes to make this word a mere qualification of the preceding,

<!-- PAGE 67 -->

<span style="color:#800000">*God-abhorred detractors*</span>. This, however, is out of keeping with the whole passage. The great majority of commentators adopt the active sense. Then follow three designations, expressive of the different forms of pride, <span style="color:#0000d4">ὑβρισταί</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*the insolent*</span>; <span style="color:#0000d4">υπερήφανοι</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*the self-conceited*</span>; <span style="color:#0000d4">ἀλαζόνυς</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*boasters*</span>: <span style="color:#0000d4">ἐφευρεταὶ</span> <span style="color:#0000d4">κακῶν</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*inventors of crimes*</span>; <span style="color:#0000d4">γονεῦσιν</span> <span style="color:#0000d4">ἀπειθεῖς</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*disobedient to parents*</span>. That such should be included in this fearful list, shows the light in which filial disobedience is regarded by the sacred writers. In ver. 31, all the words begin with the <span style="color:#0000d4">ἀ</span> privative, <span style="color:#0000d4">ἀσυνέτους</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*without*</span> (<span style="color:#0000d4">σύνεσις</span>) insight into moral or religious things, i.e., blinded, besotted, so as to think evil good, and good evil; <span style="color:#0000d4">ἀσυνθέτους</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*perfidious*</span>; <span style="color:#0000d4">ἀστόργους</span> those in whom the natural affection for parents or children is suppressed; <span style="color:#0000d4">ἀσπόνδους</span> <span style="color:#800000">*implacable*</span>; <span style="color:#0000d4">ἀνελεήμονας</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*without pity.*</span>

<!-- PAGE 68 -->
VERSE 32<span style="color:#800000">*. Who well knowing the righteous judgment of God*</span>; that is, <span style="color:#800000">*although they well know*</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*etc.*</span> They were <span style="color:#800000">*(*</span><span style="color:#0000d4">οἵτινες</span><span style="color:#800000">*) such as who.*</span> The heathen whose acts had been just described, are declared to be, <span style="color:#800000">*Men who although they knew the righteous judgment*</span>, etc., (<span style="color:#0000d4">δικαίωμα</span>) <span style="color:#800000">*decree*</span>, a declaration of what is right and just; and <span style="color:#0000d4">δικαίωμα</span> <span style="color:#0000d4">τοῦ</span> <span style="color:#0000d4">Θεοῦ</span> is the declaration of God as to what is right and just. The import of this declaration is contained in the clause, <span style="color:#800000">*that they who do*</span> (<span style="color:#0000d4">πράσσουσι</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*commit*</span>) <span style="color:#800000">*such things are worthy of death*</span>. By <span style="color:#800000">*death*</span> here, as often elsewhere, is meant punishment, in the general meaning of that word. It expresses the penalty of the law, and includes all evil inflicted for the satisfaction of justice. Paul therefore teaches that the heathen knew they deserved punishment for their crimes, or in other words, that they were justly exposed to the wrath of God, which was revealed against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men. The source of this knowledge he explains in the following chapter, ver. 14. It was a knowledge written on their hearts, or included in the constitution of their nature; it was implied in their being moral agents. As he had before shown that the impiety of the heathen was without excuse, inasmuch as they had a knowledge of the true God, so here he shows that their immorality was inexcusable, since their sins were not committed in ignorance of their nature or desert. This passage also shows that the judicial abandonment of God does not destroy the free agency or responsibility of men. They are given up to work iniquity, and yet know that they deserve death for what they do. The stream which carries them away is not without, but within. It is their own corrupt nature. It is themselves. Notwithstanding this knowledge of the ill-desert of the crimes above enumerated, <span style="color:#800000">*they not only commit them*</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*but approve of those who do*</span> (or practice) <span style="color:#800000">*them*</span>. This is the lowest point of degradation. To sin, even in the heat of passion, is evil; but to delight in the sins of others, shows that men are of set purpose and fixed preference, wicked. Such is the apostle’s argument to prove that the heathen are all under sin, that they are justly chargeable with ungodliness and unrighteousness, and consequently exposed to the wrath of God.

<p style="text-align:center" markdown="1"><span style="color:#0000d4">**DOCTRINE**</span></p>

<span class="enum-num">1.</span> The punitive justice of God is an essential attribute of his nature. This attribute renders the punishment of sin necessary, and is the foundation of the need of a vicarious atonement in order to the pardon of sinners. This doctrine the apostle assumes as a first principle, and makes it the basis of his whole exposition of the doctrine of justification, ver. 18.

<span class="enum-num">2.</span> That sin is a proper object of punishment, and that, under the righteous government of God, it will be punished, are moral axioms, which have “a self-evidencing light,” whenever proposed to the moral sense of men, vers. 18, 32.

<span class="enum-num">3.</span> God has never left himself without a witness among his rational creatures. Both in reference to his own nature and to the rule of duty, he has, in his works and in the human heart, given sufficient light to render the impiety and immorality of men inexcusable, vers. 19, 20, 32.

<span class="enum-num">4.</span> Natural religion is not a sufficient guide to salvation. What individual or what nation has it ever led to right views of God or of his law? The experience of the whole world, under all the variety of circumstances in which men have existed, proves its insufficiency; and, consequently, the necessity of a special divine revelation, vers. 21-23.

<span class="enum-num">5.</span> The heathen, who have only the revelation of God in his works and in their own hearts, aided by the obscure traditionary knowledge which has come down to them, need the gospel. In point of fact, the light which they enjoy does not lead them to God and holiness, vers. 21-23.

<!-- PAGE 69 -->

<span class="enum-num">6.</span> Error (on moral and religious subjects) has its root in depravity. Men are ignorant of God and duty, because they do not like to retain him in their knowledge, vers. 21, 28.

<span class="enum-num">7.</span> God often punishes one sin by abandoning the sinner to the commission of others. Paul repeats this idea three times, vers. 24, 26, 28. This judicial abandonment is consistent with the holiness of God and the free agency of man. God does not impel or entice to evil. He ceases to restrain. He says of the sinner, Let him alone, vers. 24-28.

<span class="enum-num">8.</span> Religion is the only true foundation, and the only effectual safeguard for morality. Those who abandon God, he abandons. Irreligion and immorality, therefore, have ever been found inseparably connected, vers. 24-28.

<span class="enum-num">9.</span> It evinces, in general, greater depravity to encourage others in the commission of crimes, and to rejoice in their commission, than to commit them one’s self, ver. 32.

<span class="enum-num">10.</span> The most reprobate sinner carries about with him a knowledge of his just exposure to the wrath of God. Conscience can never be entirely extirpated, ver. 32.

<p style="text-align:center" markdown="1"><span style="color:#0000d4">**REMARKS**</span></p>

<span class="enum-num">1.</span> It lies in the very nature of sin, that it should be inexcusable, and worthy of punishment. Instead, therefore, of palliating its enormity, we should endeavor to escape from its penalty, vers. 18, 32.

<span class="enum-num">2.</span> As the works of God reveal his eternal power and Godhead, we should accustom ourselves to see in them the manifestations of his perfections, vers. 18-21.

<!-- PAGE 70 -->
<span class="enum-num">3.</span> The human intellect is as erring as the human heart. We can no more find truth than holiness, when estranged from God; even as we lose both light and heat, when we depart from the sun. Those, in every age have sunk deepest into folly, who have relied most on their own understandings. “In thy light only, God, can we see light,” ver. 21, etc.

<span class="enum-num">4.</span> If the sins of the heathen, committed under the feeble light of nature, be inexcusable, how great must be the aggravation of those committed under the light of the Scriptures, ver. 20.

<span class="enum-num">5.</span> As the light of nature is insufficient to lead the heathen to God and holiness, it is one of the most obvious and urgent of our duties to send them the light of the Bible, vers. 20-23.

<span class="enum-num">6.</span> Men should remember that their security from open and gross sins is not in themselves, but in God; and they should regard as the worst of punishments, his withdrawing for them his Holy Spirit, vers. 24-28.

<span class="enum-num">7.</span> Sins of uncleanness are peculiarly debasing and demoralizing. To be preserved from them is mentioned in Scripture as a mark of the divine favor, Ecclesiastes 7:26; Proverbs 22:14; to be abandoned to them, as a mark of reprobation.

<span class="enum-num">8.</span> To take pleasure in those who do good, makes us better; as to delight in those who do evil, is the surest way to become even more degraded than they are themselves, ver. 32.

<!-- PAGE 71 -->

<p class="title-block-h2" style="text-align:center; font-size:16px; font-weight:bold; margin:18px 0 12px;" markdown="1"><span style="color:#006411">CHAPTER II.</span></p>

<p style="text-align:center" markdown="1"><span style="color:#0000d4">**CONTENTS**</span></p>

THE OBJECT OF THIS CHAPTER IS TO ESTABLISH THE SAME CHARGES AGAINST THE JEWS, WHICH HAD JUST BEEN PROVED AGAINST THE GENTILES; TO SHOW THAT THEY ALSO WERE EXPOSED TO THE WRATH OF GOD. IT CONSISTS OF THREE PARTS. THE FIRST CONTAINS AN EXHIBITION OF THOSE SIMPLE PRINCIPLES OF JUSTICE UPON WHICH ALL MEN ARE TO BE JUDGED, VERS. 1-16. THE SECOND IS AN APPLICATION OF THESE PRINCIPLES TO THE CASE OF THE JEWS, VERS. 17-24. THE THIRD IS AN EXHIBITION OF THE TRUE NATURE AND DESIGN OF CIRCUMCISION, INTENDED TO SHOW THAT THE JEWS COULD NOT EXPECT EXEMPTION ON THE GROUND OF THAT RITE, VERS. 25-39.

<h2 class="scripture-anchor" id="romans-2-1-16" data-ref="ROMANS 2:1-16" style="display:none">ROMANS 2:1-16</h2>

<p style="text-align:center" markdown="1"><span style="color:#0000d4">**ANALYSIS**</span></p>

## THAT men so impious and immoral, as those described in the preceding

<!-- PAGE 72 -->
chapter, deserved the divine displeasure, and could never, by their own works, secure the favor of God, the Jew was prepared readily to admit. But might there not be a set of men, who, in virtue of some promise on the part of God, or of the performance of some special duties, could claim exemption from the execution of God’s purpose to punish all sin? To determine this point, it was necessary to consider a little more fully the justice of God, in order to see whether it admitted of impunity to sinners on the ground supposed. This first section of the chapter, therefore, is employed in expanding the principle of ver. 18 of the first chapter. It contains a development of those principles of justice which commend themselves at once to every man’s conscience. The first is, that he who condemns in others what he does himself, does thereby condemn himself, ver. 1. The second, that God’s judgments are according to the truth or real state of the case, ver. 2. The third, that the special goodness of God, manifested towards any individual or people, forms no ground of exemption from merited punishment; but being designed to lead them to repentance, when misimproved aggravates their condemnation, vers. 3-5. The fourth, that the ground of judgment is the works, not the external relations or professions of men: God will punish the wicked and reward the good, whether Jew or, without the least respect of persons, vers. 6-11. The fifth, that the standard of Judgment is the light which men have severally enjoyed. Those having a written law shall be judged by it, and those who have only the law written on their hearts, (and that the heathen have such a law is proved by the operations of the, conscience, vers. 13-15,) shall be judged by that law, ver. 12. These are the principles according to which all men are to be judged in the last day, by Jesus Christ, ver. 16.

<p style="text-align:center" markdown="1"><span style="color:#0000d4">**COMMENTARY**</span></p>

<!-- PAGE 73 -->
VERSE 1. In order to appreciate the force of the apostle’s reasoning in this and the following verses, it should be remembered that the principal ground on which the Jews expected acceptance with God, was the covenant which he had made with their father Abraham, in which he promised to be a God to him and to his seed after him. They understood this promise to secure salvation for all who retained their connection with Abraham, by the observance of the law and the rite of circumcision. They expected, therefore, to be regarded and treated not so much as individuals, each being dealt with according to his personal character, but as a community to whom salvation was secured by the promise made to Abraham. Paul begins his argument at a distance; he states his principles in such general terms, that they could not fail to secure the assent of the Jew, before he was aware of their application to himself. That the Jews are addressed in this chapter is evident from the whole strain of the argument, and from the express application of the reasoning to the case of the Jews, from ver. 17 onward. This view of the passage is now generally adopted, though many of the earlier commentators supposed either that no particular class of persons is here addressed, or that the apostle has in view the better portion of the heathen, or at least those who did not seem to approve of the crimes mentioned in the preceding chapter, but rather condemned them.

The connection between this chapter and what precedes, as indicated by the particle <span style="color:#0000d4">διὸ</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*wherefore*</span>, is somewhat doubtful. Some suppose the inference to be drawn from the doctrine taught from ver. 18 of the preceding chapter. God is just, and determined to punish all unrighteousness and ungodliness of men; wherefore they are without excuse who commit the sins which they condemn in others. In this case, however, the conclusion is not exactly in the firm suited to the premises. It is not so much the inexcusableness of sinners as the exposure to punishment, that follows from the justice of God. Most commentators, therefore, consider the inference as drawn from the last verse of the preceding chapter. It is there said that all men knew that those who sin are worthy of death; and the inference is, that they which commit sin are without excuse, however censorious their self-conceit may render them towards others. <span style="color:#800000">*Every one who judges*</span>. Though from what follows it is plain that the Jews are here intended, yet for the reasons above stated the proposition is made general. <span style="color:#0000d4">Κρίνων</span> <span style="color:#800000">*judging*</span>; but by implication, condemning. <span style="color:#800000">*For wherein thou judgest another*</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*thou condemnest thyself. Wherein*</span> (<span style="color:#0000d4">ἐν ῳ</span>) either <span style="color:#800000">*in the thing which*</span>, or <span style="color:#800000">*thereby*</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*i.e.*</span>, in the same judgment, or <span style="color:#800000">*whilst*</span> See Mark 2:19; John 5:7. The reason of this assertion is given in the following clause, for thou that judgest doest the same things. It is the thing done which is the ground of condemnation; and therefore he who condemns the act, condemns the agent, whether the agent be himself or someone else, whether he be a Jew or a Gentile.

<!-- PAGE 74 -->
VERSE 2. <span style="color:#800000">*But we know*</span>. That is, however perverse and partial may be the judgment you pass on yourself, we know, etc. <span style="color:#800000">*We*</span> does not refer to the Jews, as peculiarly instructed, but to all men. Everyone knows. The proposition contained in this verse is: <span style="color:#800000">*The judgment of God is against those who do such things*</span>. That is, however they may excuse themselves, God will judge them. The words <span style="color:#0000d4">κατὰ ἀλήθειαν</span> therefore, do not form the predicate of the sentence, as though the sense were, The judgment of God is according to truth. The meaning rather is, the judgment of God, which is according to truth, is against those, etc. There are two things therefore asserted, the certainty of this divine judgment, and its being according to truth, <span style="color:#800000">*i.e.*</span>, without error, without respect of persons. It is not founded upon mere appearances or professions, but upon the real truth of the case. Comp. Proverbs 29:14, <span style="color:#0000d4">ἐν ἀληθείᾳ κρίνων πτωχούς</span> and John 8:16, <span style="color:#0000d4">ἡ κρίσις ἡ ἐμὴ ἀληθής ἐστιν</span> This verse, then, contains the second general principle of justice, according to which all men, whether Jews or Gentiles, are to be judged. The whole hope of the Jews was founded on the assumption that the judgment of God regarding them would be guided by some other rule than truth. He was not to judge them according to their real merits, but according to their national and ecclesiastical relations, just as men now hope to be saved because they belong to the true Church.

VERSE 3. <span style="color:#800000">*But thinkest thou this*</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*O man*</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*that judgest*</span>, etc. The truth that God’s judgment is just, and will fall on those who themselves commit the sins which they condemn in others, is so plain, that the apostle exclaims at the folly of those who seem to deny it. The emphasis lies on the word <span style="color:#800000">*thou*</span>, in the middle of the verse. Dost <span style="color:#800000">*thou*</span> think that thou, a Jew, and because a Jew, shalt escape the righteous judgment of God? <span style="color:#800000">*Shalt escape*</span>, <span style="color:#0000d4">ἐκφεύξῃ</span>. “Every one,” says Bengel, “who is arraigned, <span style="color:#0000d4">φεύγει</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*tries to escape*</span>; he who is acquitted, <span style="color:#0000d4">ἐκφεύγει</span> <span style="color:#800000">*escapes*</span>.” In ver. 1, the apostle had shown that the man who did what he condemned in others, condemned himself. “If then,” as Theophylact says, “he cannot escape his own judgment, how can he escape the judgment of God? If forced to condemn ourselves, how much more will the infinitely Holy condemn us?” The ground on which this false and absurd expectation rested is mentioned in the following verse:

<!-- PAGE 75 -->
VERSE 4. <span style="color:#800000">*Or despisest thou the riches of his goodness*</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*and forbearance*</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*and long-suffering*</span>? That is, admitting the general principle, that those who do what they condemn in others are themselves exposed to condemnation, do you expect exemption on the ground of the peculiar goodness of God? That this was the expectation of the Jews is plain from the apostle’s argument here and in the following chapter, and from chap. 9 and 11. Comp. also Matthew 3:9, “Think not to say, We have Abraham to our father,” and John 8:33. <span style="color:#800000">*Despisest*</span>. To despise, <span style="color:#0000d4">καταφρονεῖν</span> is to form a low estimate of. They despise the goodness of God, who form such a wrong estimate of it, as to suppose that it gives them a license to sin; who imagine that he will not punish, either because he long forbears, or because his goodness towards us is so great that we shall escape, though others perish. The words <span style="color:#0000d4">χρηστότης ἀνοχή</span> and <span style="color:#0000d4">μακροθυμία</span> express the Divine goodness under different aspects. The first means kindness in general, as expressed in giving favors; the second, patience; the third, forbearance, slowness in the infliction of punishment. The reason why the Jews, as referred to by the apostle, and men in general, thus abuse the goodness of God, is expressed by the clause, <span style="color:#800000">*not knowing that the goodness of God leadeth thee to repentance*</span>. ’<span style="color:#0000d4">Αγνοῶν</span>, not knowing, not understanding; and here, not comprehending the true nature and design of. Men abuse the goodness of God, because they do not rightly apprehend that instead of indicating a purpose not to punish, it is designed to lead them to forsake their sins. The goodness of God leads us to repentance, because it allows us our duty towards a Being who is so kind, and because it gives us ground to hope for acceptance. “The word <span style="color:#0000d4">άγει</span> <span style="color:#800000">*leads*</span>,” says Dr. Wordsworth, Canon of Westminster, in his elegant and scholarly work on the Greek Testament, “intimates not only the will of God, but the will of man. God leads, but man <span style="color:#800000">*may*</span> refuse to be led: ‘Deus ducit volentum duci’ as Bengel says, ‘Ducit suaviter non cogit.’” Very true; but who gives the will to be led? Is there no preventing grace? Does not God work in us to will, as well as to do. Surely there is such a thing as being made willing without being forced. There is a middle ground between moral suasion on and coercion. God supersedes the necessity of forcing, by making us willing in the day of his power. The apostle, however, is not here speaking of gracious influence, but of the moral tendencies of providential dispensations.

<!-- PAGE 76 -->
VERSE 5. The goodness of God, so far from being a ground of reasonable expectation that we shall ultimately escape punishment, becomes, when abused, an aggravation of our guilt. This principle the apostle here applies to the Jews, who, through their abuse of the peculiar mercy of God, were treasuring up wrath for themselves. <span style="color:#0000d4">Κατὰ δὲ τὴν σκληρότητό σου</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*after thy hardness*</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*i.e*</span>., as might be expected from thy hardness; agreeably to its nature and degree — <span style="color:#0000d4">καὶ ἀμετανόητον καρδίαν</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*heart incapable of repentance*</span>. “’<span style="color:#0000d4">Αμετανόητος</span> vim activam habet, <span style="color:#800000">*animus*</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*qui resipicere non potest*</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*poenitere nescius.*</span> Enervat hunc locum Grotius quum explicit, <span style="color:#800000">*animus*</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*qui poenitentiam non agit*</span>.” <span style="color:#800000">*Fritzsche. To treasure up*</span> is to lay up little by little, and thus accumulate a store of anything, whether good or evil. The abusers of God’s goodness accumulate a store of wrath for themselves. ’<span style="color:#0000d4">Εν ἡμέρᾳ ὀργῆς</span> is commonly rendered <span style="color:#800000">*unto*</span> the day of wrath; but this unnecessarily gives <span style="color:#0000d4">ἐν</span> the force of <span style="color:#0000d4">εἰς</span>. It is better, with De Wette, Meyer, and others, to connect <span style="color:#0000d4">ἐν</span> with <span style="color:#0000d4">ὀργὴν</span>, ‘wrath <span style="color:#800000">*at*</span> or <span style="color:#800000">*on*</span> the day of wrath.’ They treasure up for themselves wrath at that day when wrath shall be manifested. That day is further described as the day <span style="color:#0000d4">ἀποκαλύψεως δικαιοκρισίας τοῦ Θεοῦ</span> <span style="color:#800000">*of the revelation of the righteous judgment of God*</span>. Some manuscripts insert <span style="color:#0000d4">καί</span> between <span style="color:#0000d4">ἀποκαλύψεως</span> and <span style="color:#0000d4">δικαιοκρισίας</span>; which reading is preferred by Bengel, Wetstein, Mill, and Knapp. The sense then is, <span style="color:#800000">*the day of revelation*</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*and of the righteous judgment of God*</span>. The day of revelation, <span style="color:#800000">*viz*</span>., of Christ, whose second coming is always associated in Scripture with the final judgment; and therefore the day of revelation may well express the day of judgment. But as the phrase, “day of revelation” nowhere else occurs in this sense, and as the oldest manuscripts are in favor of the common text, it should be allowed to stand.

VERSE 6. <span style="color:#800000">*Who will render to every man according to his works*</span>. This is the fourth important principle which the apostle teaches us regulates the judgment of God. He will judge men neither according to their professions nor their relations, but according to their works. The question at his bar will be, not whether a man is a Jew or a Gentile, whether he belongs to the chosen people or to the heathen world, but whether he has obeyed the law. This principle is amplified and applied in what follows, in vers. 7-11. The question has been asked, how the declaration that God will render to every man, whether Jew or Gentile, according to his works — to the good, eternal life, to the wicked, indignation and wrath — is to be reconciled with the apostle’s doctrine, that no man is justified by works, that righteousness and life are not by works, but by faith, and through grace. In answering this question, two things are to be born in mind. The first is, that notwithstanding the doctrine of gratuitous justification, and in perfect consistency with it, the apostle still teaches that the retributions of eternity are according to our works. The good only are saved, and the wicked only are condemned. “For we must all appeal before the judgment-seat of Christ, that every one may receive the things done in his body, whether good or bad,” 2 Corinthians 5:10, Ephesians 6:8.

<!-- PAGE 77 -->

“Reproborum,” says Calvin, “malitiam justa ultione si puniet Dominus, rependet illis quod meriti sunt. Rursum quia sanctificat, quos olim statuit glorificare, in illis quoque bona opera coronabit, sed non pro merito.” With this accord the words of Bernard: “Bona opera sunt via regni, non causa regnandi.” The wicked will be punished on account of their works, and according to their works; the righteous will be rewarded, not on account of, but according to their works. Good works are to them the evidence of their belonging to that class to whom, for Christ’s sake, eternal life is graciously awarded; and they are, in some sense and to some extent, the measure of that reward. But it is more pertinent to remark, in the second place, that the apostle is not here teaching the method of justification, but is laying down those general principles of justice, according to which, irrespective of the gospel, all men are to be judged. He is expounding the law, not the gospel. And as the law not only says that death is the stages of sin, but also that those who keep its precepts shall live by them, so the apostle says, that God will punish the wicked and reward the righteous. This is perfectly consistent with what he afterwards teaches, that there are none righteous; that there are none who so obey the law as to be entitled to the life which it promises; and that for such the gospel provides a plan of justification without works, a plan for saving those whom the law condemns. He is here combating the false hopes of the Jews, who, though trusting to the law, were, by the principles of the law, exposed to condemnation. This he does to drive them from this false dependence, and to show them that neither Jew nor Gentile can be justified before the bar of that God, who, while he promises eternal life to the obedient, has revealed his purpose to punish the disobedient. All, therefore, that this passage teaches is that, irrespective of the gospel, to those who either never heard of it, or who, having heard, reject it, the principle of judgment will be law.

<!-- PAGE 78 -->
VERSES 7, 8. The principle laid down in ver. 6, is here amplified. God will render eternal life to the good, indignation and wrath to the wicked, without distinction of persons; to the Jews no less than to the Gentiles. Though the sense of these verses is plain, there is great difference of opinion as to the grammatical construction. The explanation adopted by our translators is perhaps the most natural, and is the one which is most generally followed. To the verb <span style="color:#0000d4">ἀποδώσει</span> of ver. 6, belong the two accusatives <span style="color:#0000d4">ζωὴν αἰώνιον</span> and <span style="color:#0000d4">θυμὸν καὶ ὀργήν</span> and the two datives, <span style="color:#0000d4">τοῖς μὲν</span> — <span style="color:#0000d4">ζητοῦσι</span> and <span style="color:#0000d4">τοῖς δὲ ἐξ ἐριθείας</span> The accusatives <span style="color:#0000d4">δόξαν</span> <span style="color:#0000d4">καὶ τιμὴν καὶ ἀφθαρσίαν</span> then of course depend on <span style="color:#0000d4">ζητοῦσι</span> and <span style="color:#0000d4">καθ</span>’ <span style="color:#0000d4">ὑπομονὴν έργου ἀγαθοῦ</span> is an adverbial qualification. The passage then reads: “To those who through perseverance in good works, seek glory, honor, and immortality, eternal life; but to those who are contentious, indignation and wrath.” Another construction, adopted by Bengel, Fritzsche, and others, supposes that <span style="color:#0000d4">τοῖς μὲν καθ</span>’ <span style="color:#0000d4">ὑπομονὴν έργου</span> <span style="color:#0000d4">ἀγαθοῦ</span> (scil. <span style="color:#0000d4">οϋσι</span>) are to be taken together, <span style="color:#800000">*to those who are according to perseverance*</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*i.e.*</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*to those who persevere*</span>; (comp. <span style="color:#0000d4">οἱ κατὰ σάρκα = οἱ</span> <span style="color:#0000d4">σαρκικοί</span> and <span style="color:#0000d4">οἱ κατὰ Πνεῦμα = οἱ πνευματικοί</span>). The following

## clause, δόξαν — ζητοῦσι, is then in apposition with the preceding:

<!-- PAGE 79 -->
“To those who persevere in good works, seeking glory, honor and immortality, he will render eternal life.” This view of the passage is recommended by the correspondence thus established between the <span style="color:#0000d4">τοῖς</span> <span style="color:#0000d4">μὲν καθ</span>’ <span style="color:#0000d4">ὑπομονήν</span> of ver. 7, and the <span style="color:#0000d4">τοῖς δε ἐξ ἐριθείας</span> of ver. 8. It is opposed, however, by the following considerations: 1. The interpretation of the phrase <span style="color:#0000d4">οἱ καθ</span>’ <span style="color:#0000d4">ὑπομονὴν έργου ἀγαθοῦ</span> is hardly born out by a reference to the phrases of <span style="color:#0000d4">οἱ κατὰ σάρκα</span> and <span style="color:#0000d4">οἱ κατὰ Πνεῦμα</span>. 2. The second clause of ver 7, if a mere amplification of the first clause, should be introduced by <span style="color:#0000d4">καὶ</span>, as in ver. 8: <span style="color:#0000d4">Τοῖς δὲ ἐριθείας καὶ</span> <span style="color:#0000d4">ἀπειθοῦσι</span>. Luther, after Oecumenius, translates thus: <span style="color:#800000">*Welcher geben wird*</span> Preis und Ehre und unvergägliches Wesen denen, die mit Geduld in guten Werken trachten nacn dem ewigen Leben:” Who will give glory, honor, and immortality to those who, in patient continuance in well-doing, seek eternal life.” According to this view, the accusatives <span style="color:#0000d4">δόξαν</span>, <span style="color:#0000d4">τιμὴν</span>, <span style="color:#0000d4">ἀφθαρσίαν</span>, depend upon <span style="color:#0000d4">ἀποδώσει</span>, and <span style="color:#0000d4">ζωὴν αἰώνιον</span> on <span style="color:#0000d4">ζητοῦσι</span>. But this the position of the words will hardly bear. Luther’s fluent and forcible version is effected by an entire transposition of the clauses. The construction therefore first mentioned is on the whole to be preferred. In the English version of the words <span style="color:#0000d4">καθ</span>’ <span style="color:#0000d4">ὑπομονήν κατά</span> is rendered <span style="color:#800000">*through*</span>. So also Grotius, De Wette, and others. See 1 Colossians 12:8; Ephesians 3:3, 7. Others translate it by the Latin preposition <span style="color:#800000">*secumdum*</span>, according to, or in virtue of ’<span style="color:#0000d4">Υπομονή</span> is rendered <span style="color:#800000">*patience*</span> by the Vulgate, and Luther; <span style="color:#800000">*patiens expectatio*</span>, by Beza; constancy, or patient continuance in our version. In illustration of the combination <span style="color:#0000d4">ὑπομονὴν έργου</span> <span style="color:#0000d4">ἀγαθοῦ</span> comp. <span style="color:#0000d4">ὑπομονὴ τῆς ἐλπίδος</span>, 1 Thessalonians 1:3. The sing. <span style="color:#0000d4">έργου</span> is used collectively for <span style="color:#0000d4">έργων</span>, as in Galatians 6:4; 1 Thessalonians 1:3; and elsewhere. What is immediately afterwards expressed by <span style="color:#800000">*eternal life*</span>, is here expressed by the three words, glory, honor, and immortality. The manifested excellence or splendor of the future condition of the saints is expressed by <span style="color:#0000d4">δόξα</span>; the honor due such excellence by <span style="color:#0000d4">τιμή</span> and the endless nature of their blessedness by <span style="color:#0000d4">ἀφθαρσία</span>

<!-- PAGE 80 -->
VERSE 8. <span style="color:#800000">*To those who are of contention*</span>, that is, <span style="color:#800000">*the contentious*</span>. Comp. <span style="color:#0000d4">οἱ</span> <span style="color:#0000d4">ἐκ πίστεως</span> believers; <span style="color:#0000d4">οἱ ἐκ περιτομῆς</span> <span style="color:#800000">*the circumcised*</span>; <span style="color:#0000d4">οἱ ἐκ</span> <span style="color:#0000d4">ἀκροβυστίας</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*the uncircumcised*</span>; <span style="color:#0000d4">οἱ ἐκ νόμου</span> <span style="color:#800000">*those who belong to the law*</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*legalists*</span>. Instead of the ordinary derivation of <span style="color:#0000d4">ἐριθεία</span> from <span style="color:#0000d4">έρις</span>, Rückert traces it to <span style="color:#0000d4">έριθος</span> <span style="color:#800000">*a hireling*</span>, which derivation is sustained by Tholuck, “Beiträge zur Spracherklärung des Neuen Testaments,” p. 25, and Fritzsche, Excursus to his Commentary on the second chapter of this epistle, and is now generally adopted. The signification of the word, as determined by its etymology and its classical usage is, <span style="color:#800000">*work for hire*</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*selfishness*</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*ambition*</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*party spirit*</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*malice*</span>. In the New Testament it is used several times in the same sense as in Philippians 1:16, <span style="color:#0000d4">οἱ μὲν ἐξ</span> <span style="color:#0000d4">ἐριθείας</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*some of rivalry*</span>, or malice; the antithetical expression is <span style="color:#0000d4">οἱ δὲ</span> <span style="color:#0000d4">ἐξ ἀγάπης</span>. In Philippians 2:3; it is connected with <span style="color:#0000d4">κενοδοξία</span> <span style="color:#800000">*vain glory*</span>. In James 3:14, 16, it is connected with <span style="color:#0000d4">ζῆλος</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*envy*</span>. In 2 Corinthians 12:20, it is distinguished from <span style="color:#0000d4">έρις</span>. These passages show that the scriptural usage of the word agrees with the classical. Still in the present case it seems to have a somewhat wider meaning. It is not envy, or rivalry, but malicious opposition to God and his requirements that is here expressed. This is plain from the explanatory causes that follow. The disposition expressed by <span style="color:#0000d4">ἐριθεία</span> is manifested in disobeying the truth, and obeying unrighteousness. Bretschneider therefore explains <span style="color:#0000d4">οἱ ἐξ</span> <span style="color:#0000d4">ἐριθείας</span> to mean <span style="color:#800000">*qui malitia ducti Deo*</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*i.e. rei divinae*</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*adversantur*</span>: “those who through malice oppose themselves to God.” The same interpretation is given by Reiche and De Wette, as well as by the older commentators. Who obey not the truth. ’<span style="color:#0000d4">Απειθέω</span> is <span style="color:#800000">*to refuse belief*</span>, to disbelieve, as well as to disobey. This clause therefore means, who refuse assent and obedience to the truth. ’<span style="color:#0000d4">Αλήθεια</span> is divine truth; what is true and right as to faith and practice. See 1:18. “Saepe,” says Bengel, “haec duo (<span style="color:#0000d4">ἀλήθεια</span> and <span style="color:#0000d4">ἀδικία</span>) inter se opponuntur: veritas continet justitiam, et injustitia connotat mendacium.” <span style="color:#800000">*Who yield themselves to*</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*or follows unrighteousness*</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*indignation*</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*and wrath*</span>, (shall be rendered). The words <span style="color:#0000d4">θυμὸς καὶ ὀργή</span> should regularly be in the accusative, as depending on <span style="color:#0000d4">ἀποδώσει</span> of ver. 6; but as they are in the nominative, <span style="color:#0000d4">έσται</span> or <span style="color:#0000d4">ἀποδώσεται</span> must be supplied. There may be, as some suppose, force in the change of construction and omission of the verb. God gives eternal life; indignation and wrath come as earned by man, so to speak, <span style="color:#800000">*Deo nolente*</span>. God wills all men to be saved. Comp. Romans 6:23. Both words are used for the sake of intensity. As to their specific difference, both ancient and modern philologists differ. The majority make <span style="color:#0000d4">θυμός</span> express the momentary impulse of anger, <span style="color:#0000d4">ὀργή</span> the permanent feeling. Others make <span style="color:#0000d4">ὀργή</span> to include the desire of vengeance, and therein to differ from <span style="color:#0000d4">θυμός</span> The former distinction is more in accordance with the primary meaning of the words; as <span style="color:#0000d4">θυμός</span> means the mind as the seat of the emotions, and hence is used for any strong passion, and <span style="color:#0000d4">ὀργή</span> means disposition, habit of mind.

<!-- PAGE 81 -->
VERSE 9. <span style="color:#800000">*Tribulation and anguish*</span>; <span style="color:#0000d4">θλῖψις</span>, (from <span style="color:#0000d4">θλίβω</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*to press*</span>,) means <span style="color:#800000">*pressure*</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*affliction*</span>; <span style="color:#0000d4">στενοχωρία</span> <span style="color:#800000">*straitness of place*</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*anguish*</span>. They are often associated; see chap. 8:35; 2 Corinthians 6:4. The latter is the stronger of the two terms, as may be inferred from its always following the other, and especially from 2 Corinthians 4:8, <span style="color:#0000d4">θλιβόμενοι</span>, ’<span style="color:#0000d4">αλλ</span>’ <span style="color:#0000d4">οὐ</span> <span style="color:#0000d4">στενοχωρούμενοι</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*troubled but not distressed*</span>; <span style="color:#800000">*Every soul of man*</span>, that is, every man. Comp. Acts 2:43; Romans 8:1, and the Hebrew <span style="color:#008080">vp,n,AlK;</span> <span style="color:#008080">µd:a:</span>; Rückert, Meyer, and others, give <span style="color:#0000d4">ψυχή</span> its full force, <span style="color:#800000">*upon every soul that belongs to a man*</span>, to express the idea that the soul and not the body is to suffer the penalty. But in 13:1, <span style="color:#0000d4">ψυχή</span> evidently stands for the whole person: ‘let every soul,’ means let every person; and such is a common scriptural meaning of the word, “if a soul sin,” “if a soul lie,” “if the priest buy a soul with his money,” etc. <span style="color:#800000">*Of the Jew first*</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*and also of the Greek*</span>. It becomes now apparent that the apostle, in laying down these general principles of justice, had the Jews specially in view. God, he says, will render to every man according to his works, to the good, eternal life; to the evil, tribulation and anguish. And lest the <span style="color:#800000">*every man*</span> should fail to arrest attention, he adds expressly, that the Jew as well as the Greek is to be thus judged. The word <span style="color:#0000d4">πρῶτον</span> may express either order or preeminence. If the former, the sense is what is expressed by Calvin, “Haec universalis est divini judicii lex, qua a Judaeis incipiet, et comprehendet totum orbem.” The judgment shall begin with the Jews, and extend to the Gentiles. If the latter, the sense is, The Jew shall not only be punished as certainly as others, but more severely, because he has been more highly favored. “The Jew first,” is equivalent then to the Jew especially. The same remark applies to the following verse. If the Jew is faithful, he shall be specially rewarded. What is true of all men, is specially true of those to whom God has revealed himself in a peculiar manner.

VERSE 10. <span style="color:#800000">*But*</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*glory*</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*honor and peace*</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*to every one doing good*</span>; <span style="color:#800000">*to the Jews first*</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*and also to the Greek*</span>. This verse completes the statement of the principle of law announced in ver. 6. The law, while it threatens death to the transgressor, promises life to the obedient; and it matters not in either case, whether it is a Jew or Gentile who receives its award. Glory, honor and peace are descriptive terms for eternal life. It is a life glorious in itself; an object of reverence or regard to others, and a source of unspeakable blessedness or peace.

VERSE 11. <span style="color:#800000">*For there is no respect of persons with God*</span>. He is righteous and impartial, looking not at the person, but the conduct of those whom he judges. This is the ground of the assurance that he will judge Jews and Gentiles according to their works. The words <span style="color:#0000d4">προσωποληψία</span> <span style="color:#0000d4">προσωπολήπτης προσωποληπτὲω</span>, are all peculiar to the New Testament, and all owe their origin to the phrase <span style="color:#0000d4">πρόσωπον λαμβάνειν</span>, which is used in the sense of the Hebrew phrase, <span style="color:#008080">µynIp: ac;n:</span>, to lift up, or accept the face of any one, that is, to be favorable to him. This is sometimes used in a good sense, as Genesis 32:20, “Peradventure he will accept of me,” literally, <span style="color:#800000">*lift up my face*</span>. Genesis 19:21; Job 42:8. Most frequently in a bad sense, for partiality. Hence judges are forbidden to accept the face of any one, Leviticus 19:15; Deuteronomy 10:17. In the New Testament, all the expressions above mentioned are used in the sense of unjust partiality. All <span style="color:#0000d4">προσωποληψία</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*respect of persons*</span>, is denied to God, and forbidden to men. See Ephesians 6:9; Colossians 3:25; James 2<span style="color:#800000">*:*</span>1.

<!-- PAGE 82 -->
VERSE 12. In the preceding verse it was stated that God is just and impartial in all his judgments. This is confirmed not only by the previous assertion, that he will judge every man according to his works, but also by the exhibition of that important principle contained in this verse. Men are to be judged by the light they have severally enjoyed. The ground of judgment is their works; the rule of judgment is their knowledge. For as many as sinned without law. That is, God is impartial, <span style="color:#800000">*for*</span> he will judge men according to the light which they have enjoyed. Our Lord teaches the same doctrine when he says, “The servant which knew his lord’s will,... shall be beaten with many stripes; but he that knew not, and did commit things worthy of stripes, shall be beaten with few stripes.” Luke 12:47, 48. <span style="color:#800000">*By law*</span>, is here meant a written or supernaturaly revealed law. In 1 Corinthians 9:21, the heathen are called <span style="color:#0000d4">άνομοι</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*without law*</span>, as distinguished from the Jews, who were <span style="color:#0000d4">ὑπὸ νόμον</span> <span style="color:#800000">*under law*</span>. <span style="color:#0000d4">Νόμος</span>, as used by the apostle, means <span style="color:#800000">*the rule of duty*</span>, the will of God revealed for our obedience; commonly, however, with special reference to the revelation made in the Scriptures. ’<span style="color:#0000d4">Ανόμως</span> is equivalent to <span style="color:#0000d4">χωρὶς νόμου</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*without law*</span>, and is not to be taken in its moral sense, <span style="color:#800000">*without restraint*</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*i.e.*</span> recklessly. ’<span style="color:#0000d4">Ανόμως καὶ ἀπολοῦνται</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*shall also persist without law*</span>, that is, their punishment shall be assigned without reference to the written law. <span style="color:#0000d4">Καί</span> before <span style="color:#0000d4">ἀπολοῦνται</span> says Rückert and Tholuck, indicates the relation between the cause and effect, or premise and conclusion; or as Fritzsche says, “necessitatem indicat, quâ <span style="color:#0000d4">τὸ ἀνόμως ἀπόλλυσθαι</span> ex <span style="color:#0000d4">τῳ ἀνόμως</span> <span style="color:#0000d4">ἁμαρτάνειν</span> consequatur.” Neither of these explanations seems to express the true force of the particle; it rather serves to indicate that as the sinning is <span style="color:#0000d4">ἀνόμως</span>, so also is the punishment. ’<span style="color:#0000d4">Απόλλυμι</span> is to <span style="color:#800000">*destroy*</span>, to put to death, spoken of physical death, and also of eternal death, Matthew 10:28; Luke 4:34; and in the passive form, Luke 13:3, 5; John 3:15, 16; 1 Corinthians 8:11. The word is strong in its own import; and as explained by other passages, it here teaches that those who sin without a written revelation — although they are to be judged fairly, and are to be treated far less severely than those who have enjoyed the light of revelation — are still to perish. “Vide igitur, quale patrocinium suscipiant, qui praeposterâ misericordiâ gentes evangelii lumine privatas ignorantiae praetextu Dei judicio eximere tentant.” <span style="color:#800000">*Calvin*</span>.

<!-- PAGE 83 -->
VERSE 13. <span style="color:#800000">*For not the hearers of the law*</span>. This verse is connected with the last clause of the preceding, and assigns the reason why the Jews shall be judged or punished according to the law; the mere possession or knowledge of the law would not avail, for it is not the hearers, but the doers of the law that are just before God. The expression <span style="color:#800000">*hearers*</span> instead of <span style="color:#800000">*readers*</span>, is explained by the fact that the law was read in the presence of the people, and by hearing rather than by reading, their knowledge of it was obtained. Comp. Matthew 5:21; John 12:34; Galatians 4:21; James 1:22. <span style="color:#800000">*To be just before God*</span>, and to be justified, are the same thing. They are both forensic expressions, and indicate the state rather than the charter of those to whom they refer. Those are just in the sight of God, or are justified, who have done what the law requires, and are regarded and treated accordingly; that is, are declared to be free from condemnation, and entitled to the favor of God. In obvious allusion to the opinion, that being a Jew was enough to secure admission to heaven, the apostle says, It is not the hearers but <span style="color:#800000">*the doers of the laws*</span> that are justified. He is not speaking of the method of justification available for sinners, as revealed in the gospel, but of the principles of justice which will be applied to all who look to the law for justification. If men rely on works, they must have works; they must be doers of the law; they must satisfy its demands, if they are to be justified by it. For God is just and impartial; he will, as a judge administering the law, judge every man, not according to his privileges, but according to his works and the knowledge of duty which he has possessed. On these principles, it is his very design to show that no flesh living can be justified.

<!-- PAGE 84 -->
VERSE 14. <span style="color:#800000">*For whenever the Gentiles*</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*not having the law*</span>. In the preceding verse the apostle had said, That not the hearers but the doers of the law are justified before God; and then adds, For whenever the Gentiles, not having the law, do by nature the things of the law, they are a law unto themselves. But the fact that the Gentiles are a law unto themselves, has nothing to do, either as an illustration or confirmation, with the general proposition contained in ver. 13. Those who insist on establishing such a connection, suppose that ver. 14 refers to the last clause of ver. 13, and is designed to prove either that with regard to the Gentiles as well as Jews, doing is the thing required; or that there are doers of the law who may be justified, among the heathen. ‘The doers of the law,’ says the apostle, ‘shall be justified; but the heathen do the law, therefore they shall be justified.’ This, however, is not the conclusion at which the apostle is aiming. He is not teaching the method of justification, or arguing to prove that the Gentiles as well as the Jews may be doers of the law, and thus be justified in the sight of God. He is expounding the law; he is showing the principles by which God will judge the world, Gentiles as well as Jews. Those who are without the written law, he will judge without any reference to that law; and those who are under the law, he will judge by that law. This general proposition he confirms first by saying, in ver. 13, that the mere possession of the law is not enough; and secondly by saying, in ver. 14, that the Gentiles have a law by which they may be judged. The logical connection of ver. 14, therefore, is not with ver. 13, but with ver. 12. Thus Calvin, who says, “Probationem prioris membri (ver. 12) nunc repetit. Probat enim frustra obtendi a gentibus ignorantiam, quum factis suis declarent, nonnullam se habere justitiae reguam. Nulla enim gens unquam sic ab humanitate abhorruit, ut non se intra leges aliquas contineret.” <span style="color:#800000">*When*</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*whenever or as often as*</span>, which may be the sense of the particle in this case, ‘Whenever, or as often as the heathen do so or so.’ Or it may have the sense of <span style="color:#800000">*while*</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*because*</span>: ‘Because, or since the heathen do so or so.’ Comp. 1 Corinthians 15:27. As <span style="color:#0000d4">έθνη</span> is without the article, many would render it <span style="color:#800000">*heathen*</span>, that is, <span style="color:#800000">*some heathen*</span>. But in the first place, it is evident from the context that this is not what the apostle means to say. His object is to show that the heathen world have a rule of duty written on their hearts; a fact which is not proved by some heathen obeying the law, but which is proved by the moral conduct of all men. Men generally, not some men, but all men, show by their acts that they have a knowledge of right and wrong. And secondly, this word has, without the article, in virtue of its frequent occurrence, a definite sense. Comp. 3:29; 9:24, and especially ver. 30: <span style="color:#0000d4">έθνη</span>.....<span style="color:#0000d4">κατέλαβε δικαιοσύνην</span>; the heathen attained righteousness. <span style="color:#800000">*Do by nature the things of the law*</span>. There are two misinterpretations of the phrase, <span style="color:#0000d4">τὰ τοῦ νόμου ποιεῖν</span>. The one is, that it means to fulfill the law; the other, to do the office of the law, <span style="color:#800000">*i.e.*</span>, to command and forbid. The former is unnecessary, and is in direct opposition to the express and repeated declaration of the apostle, that none, whether Jew or Gentile, has ever fulfilled the law. To do the things of the law, is indeed to do what the law prescribes (comp. 10:5; Galatians 3:12); but whether complete or partial obedience is intended, depends upon the context. The man who pays his debts, honors his parents, is kind to the poor, does the things of the law; for these are things which the law prescribes. And this is all the argument the apostle requires, or his known doctrine allows us to understand by the phrase, in the present instance.

<!-- PAGE 85 -->

This being the case, there is no need of resorting to the second interpretation mentioned above, which was proposed by Beza, and adopted by Wetstein, Flatt, and others. Though <span style="color:#0000d4">ποιεῖν τὰ τοῦ νόμου</span> might mean to do what the law does, prescribe what is good and forbid what is evil, it certainly has not that sense elsewhere in Paul’s writings, see 10<span style="color:#800000">*:*</span>5; Galatians 3:12; and is especially out of place here, in immediate connection with the phrase <span style="color:#0000d4">ποιηταὶ τοῦ νόμου</span> in the sense of <span style="color:#800000">*doers of the law*</span>. The heathen do <span style="color:#0000d4">φύσει</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*by nature*</span>, the things of the law. The <span style="color:#0000d4">φύσις</span> of anything is the peculiarity of its being, that in virtue of which it is what it is; it is that which belongs to its original constitution, and is opposed to what is taught, acquired, or made. The word is sometimes used for a disposition or sentiment arising out of our nature, as opposed to mere arbitrary rules, as in 1 Corinthians 11:14. In the present case, the opposition is to <span style="color:#0000d4">νόμος</span>. It is <span style="color:#800000">*by nature*</span>, not by an external law, that the Gentiles are led to perform moral acts. Comp. Galatians 4:8; Ephesians 2:3. The proper connection of <span style="color:#0000d4">φύσει</span> with <span style="color:#0000d4">τὰ τοῦ νόμου ποιῆ</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*they do by nature the things of the law*</span>, is retained in our version, and by the great majority of commentators. Bengel, Rückert, and a few others, connect it with <span style="color:#0000d4">μὴ νόμον έχοντα</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*not having the law by nature*</span>; but this saying very little to the purpose of the apostle. His object is to show that <span style="color:#0000d4">φύσις</span> supplies to the Gentiles the place of <span style="color:#0000d4">νόμος</span>. <span style="color:#800000">*These not having the law*</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*are a law unto themselves*</span>. <span style="color:#0000d4">Νόμον</span>, without the article, may be rendered either, <span style="color:#800000">*a law*</span>, “not having a law,” by implication, a written, external law; or <span style="color:#800000">*the law*</span>, <span style="color:#800000">*i.e*</span>., the Jewish law, since that word is often used without the article for the law of the Jews; that is, the law of God, as revealed in the Scriptures. The Gentiles, then, are law unto themselves; they have in their own nature a rule of duty; a knowledge of what is right, and a sense of obligation. As the absence of all moral acts among the lower animals shows that they have no sense of right and wrong, that they are not under a moral law, so the performance of such acts by the Gentiles, shows that they have a law written on their hearts.

<!-- PAGE 86 -->
VERSE 15. <span style="color:#800000">*Who show the work of the law written on their hearts*</span>. Here, as in 1:25, and often elsewhere, the relative has a causal force: ‘They are a law unto themselves, because they show the work of the law,’ etc. Wolf, Tholuck, and others make <span style="color:#0000d4">έργον τοῦ νόμου</span> a periphrase for the law itself; Grotius, the effect of the law, that is, a knowledge of right and wrong; most modern commentators make <span style="color:#0000d4">τὸ έργον</span> equivalent to <span style="color:#0000d4">τὰ έργα</span>. The same works which the Jews have prescribed in their law, the Gentiles show to be written on their hearts. It is by doing the things of the law, that the Gentiles show they have this inward rule of duty; <span style="color:#800000">*their conscience also bearing witness*</span>. Grotius, Koppe, and Tholuck, take <span style="color:#0000d4">συμμαρτυρεῖν</span> in the sense of the simple verb. Comp. Jeremiah 11:7, in the LXX., Romans 9:1; 8:16. ‘Their conscience bearing witness,’ that is, to the fact that there is a law written on their hearts. But as <span style="color:#0000d4">συμμαρτυρεῖν</span> is properly <span style="color:#800000">*una testari*</span>, and as the context presents no reason for departing from the common meaning of the word, the great majority of commentators give the <span style="color:#0000d4">σύν</span> its proper force. That with which conscience joins its testimony is the <span style="color:#800000">*honestas vitae*</span>, the moral acts of the heathen; and the fact to which this joint testimony is born, is that they are a law unto themselves. The apostle appeals not only to their external conduct, but to the inward operations of their moral nature. <span style="color:#0000d4">Συνείδησις</span> is the <span style="color:#800000">*conscientia consequens*</span> is, the inward judge, whose acts are described in the following clause: <span style="color:#800000">*Their thoughts alternately accusing or even excusing*</span>.
